title: Investment bankers jump ship as data centre talent war heats up
full_text:
Investment banks have become a hunting ground for talent amid a boom in artificial intelligence, with data centre developers raiding research desks and advisory teams to bankroll, build and sell a wave of new projects.
The latest to join the data centre gold rush is JPMorgan's head of technology, media and telecommunications research, Bob Chen, who resigned last week after seven years at the Wall Street giant's Sydney outpost.
According to sources, the analyst, who covered ASX-listed technology companies including NextDC, WiseTech Global and Xero, has been lured to Sydney-headquartered, Nasdaq-listed AI infrastructure developer Iren, where he will work on investor relations.
For investment banks, competition for staff, with generous compensation, is no longer coming only from rival firms or private equity.
Data centre developers are increasingly poaching staff from the banks advising them, despite Wall Street bonuses becoming more lucrative to Australian bankers because deferred equity awards benefit from soaring bank share prices and a favourable exchange rate.
But AI infrastructure companies are proving willing to pay up. On June 30, Iren disclosed that the company's founders, brothers William and Daniel Roberts, were each awarded 9 million shares that vest over four years, without performance hurdles. Based on Monday's closing share price of $US36.29, each package is worth about $US330 million ($447 million), although the stock remains well below its 52-week high of $US76.87.
Some investors have criticised the lucrative share grants, forcing Iren chairman David Bartholomew to defend them. "The market for people who can secure power, build big data centres and monetise them has never been more aggressive," he wrote in a letter to shareholders this month.
Iren's head of business development, Boris Dangubic, joined the company after leaving private equity giant CVC Capital Partners, where he was a senior managing director until March. And chief financial officer Anthony Lewis also brought extensive banking experience when he joined Iren last year after working at Macquarie for more than two decades.
Iren's founders are also Macquarie alumni. The Roberts brothers left the investment banking giant to establish the company, then known as Iris Energy, in 2018 before listing it on the Nasdaq three years later. Originally focused on bitcoin mining, Iren has reinvented itself as an AI infrastructure company and plans to dedicate data centres in North America, Australia and Europe solely to cloud services.
The transformation has been accompanied by a rush of new customers. AI search engine Perplexity, robotics company Figure AI and image generation platform Fal AI are among businesses that have signed contracts worth a combined $US2.8 billion. Iren recently lifted its forecast for cloud services revenue in 2027 to $US4 billion, up from a $US3.7 billion projection in May.
Other AI infrastructure hopefuls are following the same script.
Before its proposed Australian listing, Sharon AI has recruited long-time Macquarie technology banker Anuj Goel as chief financial officer. His package includes a $650,000 salary, an annual cash or equity bonus of up to $650,000, a long-term equity incentive worth up to $1.3 million and a $1.35 million sign-on share award that vests progressively until 2031.
Last year, the company hired Ross Burrows, the former head of technology research at Wilsons Advisory and former head of small-cap research at Citi, to oversee capital strategy and investor relations.
Firmus, which is planning a $15.5 billion ASX float, has also looked to investment banking talent, appointing former Bank of America Australian financials research head Toby Langley to lead investor relations.
One investor that has already enjoyed the ride is Regal Partners, which first backed Iren in 2019 when the company was valued at just $US24 million. Regal still holds a small stake.
